_authority: The first question is always LEARNING, never format. This file maps what a learner must understand to the representations that can carry it. decide/GUIDE.md points here and must not restate the table in prose.
_rule: Name the learning need BEFORE naming a representation. A concept whose need cannot be named does not need a visual - it needs clearer text, or it does not belong on the screen.
_reading: candidates are ordered strongest-first for that need. 'avoid' is not a ban; it is what usually teaches worse for THIS need and needs a reason if chosen.

physical_appearance.question: What does this actually look like, so I recognise it on a ship?
physical_appearance.why: A trainee who learns to recognise equipment from a stylised icon has learned something false. Recognition needs the real object.
physical_appearance.test: Could the learner pick this out of a row of similar equipment after seeing it?

location.question: Where is it, on the ship or in the system?
location.why: Location is spatial. A list of place names does not build a spatial model.
location.test: Could the learner point at it on a drawing they have not seen before?

internal_structure.question: What is inside it, that I cannot see from outside?
internal_structure.why: No camera can see inside a sealed containment system. This is the classic case for a drawing - and the page must say on its face that it is a drawing.
internal_structure.test: Does the learner understand what is behind the surface they can see?

system_relationships.question: How do these parts connect, and what depends on what?
system_relationships.why: A real system has topology - services, headers, branches, direction. Boxes in a row assert a false linearity.
system_relationships.test: Could the learner say what happens downstream if one element is shut?

flow.question: What moves, where does it go, and in which direction?
flow.why: Direction and path are the content. A static arrow states a conclusion; a traced path lets the learner follow it.
flow.test: Could the learner trace the route with a finger and say where it ends?

sequence.question: What happens in what order, and why that order?
sequence.why: Order is the content. Cards side by side imply simultaneity.
sequence.test: Could the learner say why step 3 cannot come before step 2?

state_change.question: What is different before and after, and what caused the change?
state_change.why: A single state cannot show a change. Two states, or a controlled transition between them, can.
state_change.test: Could the learner name the two states and the thing that moved between them?

mechanism.question: How does it actually work, internally?
mechanism.why: Mechanism is the strongest case for animation in the whole system: several properties changing together, causally.
mechanism.test: Could the learner predict what happens if one input changes?

cause_and_effect.question: What follows from what, and what breaks the chain?
cause_and_effect.why: Causation needs an ordered reveal so the learner sees the link form, not a finished diagram of it.
cause_and_effect.test: Could the learner say where an intervention would stop it?

comparison.question: How do these differ, and which do I have in front of me?
comparison.why: Differences are seen, not read. Show the variants against the same viewpoint and scale so the difference is the only thing that changes.
comparison.test: Could the learner tell two of them apart in a photograph?

hazard.question: What is dangerous here, and what does it do to me?
hazard.why: A hazard icon names a category. It does not teach recognition or consequence. Use semantic hazard colour from course-module-ui, never a stock warning glyph as the whole content.
hazard.test: Could the learner spot it in a scene that was not staged for them?

trend.question: How does one quantity move with another?
trend.why: A relationship between two quantities is a chart. Never draw a curve that is not built from sourced values.
trend.test: Could the learner read a value off it, and say where the source stops and interpolation begins?

decision.question: Given this situation, what do I do, and why?
decision.why: A decision is practised, not watched. This is usually a task screen, not a deck screen - route it to course-task-ux.
decision.test: Did the learner have to commit to an answer?

troubleshooting.question: It is not behaving. What is wrong?
troubleshooting.why: Troubleshooting needs a system the learner can perturb and a readable symptom. Usually a task screen.
troubleshooting.test: Could the learner localise the fault rather than name it?

procedure.question: What are the steps, in order, and what does 'done' look like?
procedure.why: A procedure a learner will perform is often best as clear ordered text plus one photograph per non-obvious step. Animating it adds nothing they can carry to the deck.
procedure.test: Could the learner follow it with their hands, without the screen?

plain_text_is_a_valid_decision.rule: Choosing NO visual is a real outcome of this process and must be recorded in the storyboard with its reason, exactly like any other choice.
when: the content is a definition, a limit, a name or a rule - text carries it exactly and a picture would only decorate it
the learner needs the exact wording (a regulatory phrase, a set point, a criterion)
a visual would restate the sentence beside it without adding a relationship, a location or a change
the concept is genuinely abstract and every candidate visual would be a metaphor the learner then has to unlearn
plain_text_is_a_valid_decision.anti_rule: Never add a visual to fill space, to make a screen look finished, or because a screen 'needs' an image. An empty area is cheaper than a misleading one.
